query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, the unstable passive film on the multiphase eutectic high-entropy alloy—particularly on the corrosion‐sensitive Al-Ni-rich phase—breaks down. This film degradation, accelerated by mechanical wear which mechanically removes any nascent passive film, exposes fresh, reactive metal that undergoes rapid localized corrosion. This creates a synergistic feedback loop where wear aggravates corrosion and vice versa, leading to an overall degradation rate that is higher than the sum of its individual wear and corrosion contributions.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) featuring a lamellar microstructure with alternating phases including an Al-Ni-rich phase that initially forms a protective passive film composed of mixed hydroxides and oxides.
generation.intervention: Expose alloy samples to simultaneous wear and corrosive attack at elevated temperature in a chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution. A set of control samples will be exposed to only wear or only corrosion under the same temperature and solution conditions.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., 50–100 °C) in a corrosive medium containing chloride ions (such as a diluted sulfuric acid solution), under defined mechanical sliding/contact conditions that impose controlled wear on the surface. The microstructure must include phases with inherently different film stabilities.
generation.structural_mediator: The breakdown of the passive film on the Al-Ni-rich phase and potential differential stability among the phases (e.g., L12 versus B2) that leads to localized film rupture and enhances the exposure of reactive surfaces.
generation.mechanism: Temperature-induced instability modifies the composition of the passive film (altering the ratios of hydroxides and oxides for Fe and Cr), making it less protective. Under wear, this weakened film is mechanically removed, exposing the underlying metal which then undergoes accelerated local corrosion. The corrosion further undermines the mechanical integrity of the surface, thus speeding up wear in a mutually reinforcing manner.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under combined exposure, the total material degradation (mass loss, pitting density, and surface roughening) will be significantly greater than the additive effects of isolated wear and corrosion. Specifically, wear loss will be higher due to the diminished surface integrity, and corrosion damage (e.g., pitting depth and density) will be increased in regions where wear has removed the protective film.
generation.baseline: A matched alloy sample tested either at a lower temperature (where the passive film remains stable) or under isolated wear or corrosion conditions, ensuring all other parameters (composition, microstructure, loading) remain constant.
generation.boundary: The proposed synergistic degradation is expected only in corrosive environments with chloride ions and above a critical temperature that destabilizes the passive film. In inert or less aggressive environments, or at lower temperatures, the protective film remains stable and the accelerated coupling effect should not manifest.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitatively, the precise contributions of wear versus corrosion in the synergy remain uncertain, as does the threshold temperature for passive film breakdown; variations in alloy microstructure or environmental aggressiveness could shift these parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples with identical lamellar microstructures. Subject one set to simultaneous tribocorrosion testing (combining controlled wear with electrochemical exposure at the specified elevated temperature) and the other set to separate wear‐only and corrosion‐only tests under the same temperature and solution conditions. Compare total mass loss, surface pitting, and electrochemical response between the combined and isolated tests.
measurements: Surface morphology analysis (using SEM and pitting density/counts)
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (to assess passive film integrity)
XPS or similar surface analysis (to detect film composition changes)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the total degradation under simultaneous wear and corrosion does not significantly exceed (i.e., is merely the sum of) the degradation from the isolated wear and corrosion tests, or if surface analysis shows no evidence of passive film breakdown (i.e., unchanged film composition or integrity), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Corrosion Behavior of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy in Chloride-Containing Sulfuric Acid Solutions at Different Temperatures

Abstract: In this work, the influence of temperature on the corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in a chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution was investigated using electrochemical measurement, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and scanning electron microscopy. Results show that the passive film of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 is stable in chloride-containing sulfuric acid solutions at low temperatures, while an unstable film forms on the alloy at high temperatures. Furthermore, temperature changes the proportion of hydroxide and oxide in Fe and Cr, but it has no noticeable effect on Al and Ni, which is a significant factor on the passive behavior. L12 phase exhibits good corrosion resistance at different temperatures. Pitting occurred on B2 phase in the chloride-containing sulfuric acid solution at a low temperature of 5 °C, while pitting and dissolution take place on AlCoCrFeNi2.1 in the acid solution at room temperature and above.

Conclusions: The effect of temperature on the passive and corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi2.1
